sections.markdown:
## C — Sharing the road: motorcycles, large trucks and the No-Zone, pedestrians, bicycles and mopeds, electric bicycles, funeral processions, road rage, reporting drunk drivers and littering
Knowledge domain: how a car driver shares lanes and space with motorcycles, tractor-trailers, pedestrians, bicyclists and moped riders, which equipment and licenses those riders need, how to treat a funeral procession, how to respond to road rage, and when to report a drunk driver.

FACT_ID: sec05-F01 | anchor: A01
Drivers often fail to notice motorcycles, and judging how fast or how far away a motorcycle is can be hard. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F02 | anchor: A01
Never share a lane with a motorcycle, because the rider needs the whole lane to stay safe. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F03 | anchor: A01
When passing a motorcycle, give it a full lane width instead of squeezing by, and wait for a clear stretch if the lane is too narrow to share. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F04 | anchor: A01
Riders shift speed and lane position for manhole covers, diagonal rail tracks, debris or strong wind, so be ready to react when you follow one. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F05 | anchor: A01
Missouri law requires motorcycle riders to wear a helmet. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F06 | anchor: A01
Riding a motorcycle on public streets requires a valid driver license with a motorcycle endorsement, or a motorcycle license. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F07 | anchor: A02
A typical tractor-trailer can weigh as much as 80,000 pounds, and with a long trailer the whole rig can be longer than 90 feet. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F08 | anchor: A02
Do not pull onto a road in front of a large vehicle, and avoid moving over in front of one when you are about to turn off the road. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F09 | anchor: A02
If you cannot see a truck or bus driver in that vehicle's rearview mirrors, the driver cannot see you either. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F10 | anchor: A02
The No-Zone is the set of blind spots beside, behind and in front of a truck or bus where a car disappears from view, so stay out of it unless it is truly necessary. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F11 | anchor: A02
Do not ride alongside a large vehicle for long stretches, and do not tailgate one; keep a safety cushion around it. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F12 | anchor: A02
After passing a truck, wait until you can see its cab in your rearview mirror before moving back in, then signal, hold your speed and do not slow down ahead of it. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F13 | anchor: A02
On steep grades, keep out of the right lane of a divided or multi-lane road where slow trucks travel, and avoid the right lane near weigh stations so trucks can merge back in. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F14 | anchor: A02
Vehicles hauling hazardous materials are required to stop at every railroad crossing, so be ready for them to stop. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F15 | anchor: A02
A large truck may swing left first to make a right turn, so watch its turn signal before you try to pass it. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F16 | anchor: A02
At 55 mph an average car stops in roughly 130 to 140 feet, while a fully loaded tractor-trailer may need almost 400 feet. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F17 | anchor: A02
Rather than cut off a truck, slow down and make your turn or lane change behind it, which costs only a few seconds. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F18 | anchor: A03
A tractor-trailer often seems slower than it really is because of its size, which leads to crashes at intersections when car drivers misjudge its distance or speed. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F19 | anchor: A03
A pedestrian facing a Walk signal or green light has the right-of-way but should start across only after making sure drivers see them and stop. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F20 | anchor: A03
A pedestrian should not start crossing on a Don't Walk signal or a red or yellow light, but someone already in the street when the Don't Walk begins flashing may finish crossing. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F21 | anchor: A03
Pedestrians should use an intersection or crosswalk in a business district or between two close signalized intersections, and must yield to all traffic when crossing mid-block. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F22 | anchor: A03
Where there is no sidewalk, walk on the side of the road facing oncoming traffic. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F23 | anchor: A03
Even on a green light, a driver must yield to every pedestrian in the intersection, and must take care to avoid pedestrians whether or not they are obeying the law. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F24 | anchor: A03
Never pass a vehicle that has stopped or slowed for a pedestrian. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F25 | anchor: A03
Obey the lower school-zone speed limit when its lights flash or children are present, and stop if a school crossing patrol member signals you. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F26 | anchor: A04
Always yield to a blind pedestrian; when someone crosses with a guide dog or a white cane, with or without a red tip, vehicles must stop completely. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F27 | anchor: A04
Yield to a pedestrian in a marked or unmarked crosswalk who is on your side of the road or approaching it. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F28 | anchor: A04
Do not block the crosswalk while waiting at a red signal, and yield to pedestrians before driving across a sidewalk or crosswalk. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F29 | anchor: A04
Most crashes with bicycles and mopeds happen at intersections, so scan for them and give them the same consideration as any other vehicle. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F30 | anchor: A04
Before turning right onto a main road, look right as well as left for wrong-way cyclists on the road or the sidewalk. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F31 | anchor: A04
If you need to turn right while following a cyclist, slow down and stay behind the rider until you can turn. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F32 | anchor: A04
When turning left, yield to an oncoming cyclist unless you are certain you can finish the turn before the rider reaches the intersection. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F33 | anchor: A04
Give a bicycle or moped a full lane width when passing, slowing down if needed, and wait for a clear stretch if the lane is too narrow to share. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F34 | anchor: A04
A bicycle lane is a striped part of the roadway for bicycles; you may cross it to turn or to enter or leave the road, but you must yield to cyclists in it. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F35 | anchor: A04
Moped and bicycle riders have the same rights and duties as motorists on public roads and must always ride with traffic, never against it. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F36 | anchor: A05
A rider going slower than traffic generally keeps as far right as is safe, but may move toward the middle or left to turn left, avoid hazards, use a lane too narrow to share, or go straight past a right-turn-only lane. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F37 | anchor: A05
Mopeds are not allowed on any part of the federal interstate highway system. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F38 | anchor: A05
Missouri does not require moped or bicycle riders to wear a helmet, although a safety-certified one can prevent serious head injury or death. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F39 | anchor: A05
Riders passing to the left of a parked or moving vehicle should leave three to four feet of space for a door that swings open or a car that swerves. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F40 | anchor: A05
Driving a moped on public streets requires a valid driver license. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F41 | anchor: A06
Missouri does not require mopeds or bicycles to be registered or inspected, but it does require certain equipment. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F42 | anchor: A06
Moped and bicycle brakes must be able to stop the rider within 25 feet from a speed of ten mph. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F43 | anchor: A06
From half an hour after sunset until half an hour before sunrise a bicycle needs a white front light that drivers can see from 500 feet. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F44 | anchor: A06
Riding an electric bicycle that meets the state definition does not require an operator license or a motorcycle license. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F45 | anchor: A06
Every vehicle in a funeral procession uses its flashing emergency lights and follows the car ahead as closely as is safe. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F46 | anchor: A06
An organized funeral procession has the right-of-way at every intersection regardless of traffic signals, except for emergency vehicles or when police direct otherwise. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F47 | anchor: A07
Drivers outside a funeral procession may not cut between its moving vehicles, join it to get the right-of-way, or pass its vehicles except in a lane provided for passing. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F48 | anchor: A07
Road rage is an uncontrolled display of anger by a driver, usually in response to another driver, that can damage property or injure people. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F49 | anchor: A07
Faced with road rage, stay calm and do not respond in kind, note the location and descriptions of the driver and vehicle, and report it to local authorities as soon as you can. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F50 | anchor: A07
To report road rage by cellphone, first leave the road to a safe spot, then dial *55, or 911 in a metropolitan area. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F51 | anchor: A07
If you think you have seen a drunk driver, tell the police at once and give the plate number, a description of the car and driver, and its location. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F52 | anchor: A07
Littering is illegal, and a court can impose a fine of up to $1,000, up to one year in jail, or both. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0036]

Misconceptions: a green light does not let a driver go ahead while pedestrians are still in the intersection; a car may not share a lane with a motorcycle; Missouri requires a helmet for motorcycle riders but not for moped or bicycle riders; a truck that looks slow is often closer and faster than it appears.
Mnemonics: no mirror, no driver, no view, so if you cannot see the trucker in the mirror the trucker cannot see you; full lane for every two-wheeler when passing.
Glossary: No-Zone means the blind spots around a truck or bus; bicycle lane means a striped part of the road set aside for bicycles; motorized bicycle means a small-engine moped of the kind defined by state law; road rage means an uncontrolled display of anger by a driver; funeral procession means an organized line of vehicles following a funeral, using flashing emergency lights.
Dynamic facts: the littering fine and jail limits are statutory and can change, and the phone number for reporting a highway emergency should be checked against current Highway Patrol guidance.

corpus_stability.reason: The Missouri Driver Guide prints a single edition line on its front cover (Revised August 2026); its table-of-contents note says law and policy changes may make parts out of date and points to the website for the current version, with no sign in the selected pages of more than one rewrite per year.
